sections.title: A language with more than one written form

paragraphs.text: Ho is a North Munda language in the Austroasiatic family. In Odisha, the SCSTRTI profile places Ho communities in Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar and Angul. A district name helps place a community on a map, but it does not tell you which script a particular reader uses.

Warang Citi, devised by Lako Bodra, is one way of writing Ho. Unicode also records Ho writing in Devanagari, Odia and Latin. Warang Citi runs from left to right and distinguishes uppercase from lowercase. Its vowels have full letters, although consonants may also carry an unwritten vowel. That last detail matters: the appearance of separate vowel letters does not mean every vowel must appear separately on the page.

Michael Everson’s 2012 encoding proposal names two Warang Citi publications: the annual magazine Ho Sanagam and the biweekly Kolhan Sakam. These are dated examples of the script in print; their current publication schedules have not been checked. They show a use for the script beyond an alphabet chart: magazines and periodicals written for readers to return to.

The Ho–Odia Primer published by CIIL and NCERT in July 2024 takes another route, using Odia script. Its development team includes Kanda Charan Naik, Ramrai Muduiya and Jaypal Singh Naik as resource persons. The book is intended for early learning and adult literacy. These names make the work of preparing a reader visible alongside the institutions on its cover.

On printed page 6, a large letter sits beside coloured word labels and a picture of a bee on a flower. Below are mangoes, a boat and a bird, each with paired labels. At the bottom, the letter becomes progressively fainter. The page offers several things to do: look closely, compare the labels and practise the form. Its script and layout are visible even before a newcomer can read the Ho words.

The 2018 Ho booklet offers a different starting point: English, Odia and Ho in parallel columns. Its contents move from pronouns and body parts to household objects and everyday sentences. A reader can follow a familiar item across the columns, then take an unfamiliar word to a Ho speaker for its sound and use. The named compilers remain credited in the learning shelf below.

The SCSTRTI profile describes an akhara as a dancing space and a sarna as a sacred grove. Such terms connect language with particular kinds of shared place. They are a useful reason to ask how a word is used locally, rather than treating an institutional description as a complete account of every settlement.
Begin with one page or one place name. Ask the person reading with you which written form they use, what the printed example leaves out, and whether the word belongs in an everyday conversation.
